content:
Alarms can give reassurance if you live alone.

This guide covers how they work. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

How they work

Press the button to reach a response centre.

Alarm buttons when fingers are stiff or swollen

  • Choose a large, easy-press button.
  • Try it before committing.
  • Wear it at all times, including in the bathroom if waterproof.

Fall detectors

Some alarms detect falls automatically.

Getting one

Ask your council or compare providers.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is there a cost?

Usually a weekly or monthly charge.

Who responds?

A named contact or responder.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Falls
  • NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
